title: Fern's Forgotten Parcel
markdown:
Once, in a highland of tumbling waterfalls, chattering ravens, and stairways cut into ancient rock, witch Fern kept a cottage that was a charming mess: cauldrons, herb baskets, scrolls in towers. Every day she tiptoed in worn slippers through dust-mote sun, gathering dew-kissed herbs, measuring powders, sighing at a misplaced toadstool or a runaway moonpetal. Bramble the hedgehog patrolled with serious spines, sniffing moss that smelled of old earth, or a beetle that dared his path. Fern loved the quiet hum of her magic. Sometimes, when a potion bubbled over, she wished the day would surprise her—just a little.

Until one day a raven with a rusty-hinge cackle landed on the sill. Not the usual grumble about the mountain-goat council’s zoning. It dropped a parcel no bigger than a thumb, tinkling an urgent fairy-sneeze of a melody. The note, looping and flustered, was smudged with ink and possibly jam. Fern! The utterly, ridiculously, monumentally important parcel! Deliver before moonrise! You forgot!

Her heart hop-skipped. She had forgotten. The Parcel of Perpetual Punctuality, bound for the Mists of Meridia, who were famous for being on time. Moonrise was near. She pictured the Mists tapping their feet.

Because of that, the orderly day became rummaged shelves and misplaced pouches. A toadstool rolled under the table as if it had opinions about punctuality. She grabbed the parcel—oddly warm, a faint rhythmic beat—and a satchel of hastily scooped glow-worm dust like captured starlight. Bramble, smelling panic the way he smelled beetles, puffed until his spines were a fence, and nudged her boot with a determined snout.

“Right then,” Fern said, crooked hat already independent. “A very last-minute adventure. No tea. No proper sorting. Don’t look at me like that. I know.”

They scrambled down a rocky path: damp earth, crushed pine, a rumour of wild berries. Usual raven calls, which often gossiped about weather, now seemed to cheer or mock; with ravens it was hard to tell. Fern’s slippers were the wrong shoes for haste and she did not have time to be right. Rounding a bend, a colossal shadow fell, vast and sudden, midnight unfurling too soon. Ignis blocked the cliff-hugging shortcut, obsidian scales, smoke rings like hesitant clouds, one perfect wisp from a nostril. He was trying very hard to seem mysterious.

“Halt!” The boom vibrated Fern’s bones. “Who dares tread upon the path of… the unknown?” A dramatic claw-tap.

“Hello, Ignis,” Fern said, practical as a shopping list. “Lovely to see you, truly. We’re in a frightful hurry. Parcel before moonrise. You know how the Mists get. They mutter about strange time happenings, and then everyone else’s clocks feel guilty.”

Ignis’s amber eyes, molten gold in the fading light, worked at stern. A wisp escaped as he hunted for an awe-inspiring sentence. “A parcel, you say? Stolen artifact? Forbidden spell? The key to an ancient secret? One does not rush past a guardian for jam.”

“The Parcel of Perpetual Punctuality,” Fern said, flat as a well-used spoon. “Late because I forgot until a raven was rude about it. No jam. Possibly jam on the note. Not the same.”

A jaunty lute cut in. Lyric the elf, bright-eyed, sixth sense for anything that might become a ballad, struck a chord as if destiny had hired him.

“The witch Fern and hedge-friend Bramble brave the shadow of Ignis! A forgotten parcel! Names for the ages!”

Fern rolled her eyes. “Not now, Lyric. I forgot. There’s no epic in a late delivery. It’s a grocery list with better stationery.”

Ignis huffed, mystery leaking out as a sigh. “This passage is guarded. Whispering Gorge. A shortcut for the determined. One must earn passage.” He looked as if he hoped for an enchanted mushroom.

Fern’s mind raced like a squirrel with a nut. The main path around the gorge would take too long; the sun was already dipping, orange and purple like a bruise that had decided to be beautiful. The shortcut, guarded by a dragon who wanted mystery and had mostly achieved being large, might be the only hope.

“Can you let us through? It would save us so much time. The Mists are particular.”

A spark of real interest, not practised mystique, crossed Ignis’s face. He puffed his chest; scales caught the last light.

“Perhaps. If you prove worthy. And answer my riddle.” He winked, charming on such a large snout.

Lyric’s fingers flew. “The dragon’s riddle! Wit and wisdom! Heroes or forgotten time!”

“No,” Fern said. “I’m not playing riddles. I’m late. My wits are butter-knife sharp at present.” She glanced at Bramble, nose twitching. “We need the gorge. And I have a feeling you know how.”

Bramble snuffled, determined, and trotted toward a track barely wide enough for a beetle. Fern followed. Trust was a habit between them.

The track found a narrow rickety bridge over a roaring gorge, water a grey beast below, a constant thundering symphony. Damp stone, moss, sharp spray. She clutched the parcel’s warm pulse against her chest. The first plank creaked like a warning that had given up being listened to. Then a miracle of lights: thousands of glow-worms clinging under the bridge to wet rock and crevice, flickering in unison, a green carpet, a silent sparkling audience. The chasm, which had been a terror, became a wonderland.

“Oh, my,” Fern whispered. Even Lyric was silent, lute forgotten, jaw adrift.

They took another careful step. Another. Bramble’s feet made almost no sound, which was his whole philosophy. Then Fern’s foot caught a loose plank she would have seen on a less hurried day. She stumbled. The satchel of glow-worm dust—needed to wake the Fading Ferns on the far side, without which the path would stay lost—slipped and showered faint sparks toward the abyss.

“The dust!” Dismay, not a ballad. “They won’t bloom. The Mists will wait with their arms folded.”

Ignis, mystery abandoned, made a startled squawk like a goose with a stubbed toe. Then, without a pronouncement, he swooped beneath the bridge, vast wings taking the air, surprisingly agile for someone who had just been practising poses. He nudged the falling satchel back with a gentle snout, precious dust mostly intact. Helpful. Dragon-sized. No riddle attached.

Lyric recovered at once. “He who sought mystery reveals a noble heart! A champion of the forgotten parcel!”

Ignis landed, flustered. “It seemed necessary. If you are going to be mysterious,” he told Lyric, “you could at least be punctual. Being late is not mysterious. It is inconvenient.”

“Thank you,” Fern said. “Unexpectedly helpful.” Bramble’s eyes held a satisfied glint. He had seen the plank. He had known her hurry.

They stood on the far side, spray still on their faces. A pearly sliver of moon peeked over jagged peaks and laid long silver on the rock. Fern did not wait for a verse. She hurried to the Fading Ferns, fronds drooped, leaves tinged with a tired sort of sadness, and sprinkled the rescued dust as if it were a kindness rather than a spell. The ferns bloomed. A shimmering, well-lit path opened like someone remembering a promise. She ran it. The Parcel of Perpetual Punctuality met the waiting Mists of Meridia as the last sliver of moon slid behind stone. The Mists, who were always on time, accepted it without a lecture, which was as close as mists came to thanks.

Ignis looked less like a poster of mystery and more like a dragon who had been useful. He tried a wisp of smoke, then let it go. Lyric, of course, began a new tune—not of battles, of a witch who forgot, a hedgehog who remembered, and a dragon who showed up. Fern did not stay for the chorus. Bramble was already sniffing the way home, which was, she thought, the only map worth trusting.

Ever since then Fern’s highlands were a little less predictable, a lot more interesting, and filled with the quiet hum of unexpected friendships. The cottage still sighed at toadstools. Bramble still patrolled beetles and particularly interesting moss. Lyric still arrived whenever anything might scan. Sometimes Ignis blocked a path only to ask if she had remembered her parcels, smoke-ring optional, which was, in its way, the most mysterious kindness on the mountain. The air still smelled of magic and pine. Now and then it also smelled of a parcel delivered just in time, which is a smell only witches and hedgehogs truly notice.
characters: Fern (highland witch), Bramble (hedgehog companion), Ignis (a dragon who is trying very hard to seem mysterious)
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for independent readers
author: StoryGen Community
